concept.technique_name: linear pair of interior and exterior angle with exterior-angle sum

examples.problem_statement: Difference between interior and exterior angle of a polygon is 100^\circ. Then the number of sides in the polygon is: (a) 8 (b) 9 (c) 10 (d) 11

solution.result: sum equation relating the two angles
solution.description: Name the interior angle x and the exterior angle y, and write that they add to a straight angle, as the book does.
Translate the given difference between interior and exterior angle into the second equation.
Solve the pair of equations for x, the interior angle.
Solve the same pair for y, the exterior angle.
Divide the full 360 degrees of exterior angles by one exterior angle to get the number of sides.

key_reminders: An interior angle and its adjacent exterior angle form a linear pair summing to 180^\circ.
The exterior angles of any polygon total 360^\circ, so for a regular polygon n = 360^\circ / (\text{one exterior angle}).
Two linear equations in x and y (sum and difference) pin both angles down uniquely.
common_mistakes: Dividing 360 by the interior angle 140 instead of the exterior angle 40.
Reading the 100^\circ difference as one of the angles themselves rather than as x - y.

concept.technique_name: average speed as total distance over total time

examples.problem_statement: Jack traveled the first 75% of an 80-mile trip at 45 miles per hour and the remainder at 30 miles per hour. What was Jack's average speed for the entire 80-mile trip, in miles per hour? (A) 37.5 (B) 38.25 (C) 40 (D) 41.25 (E) 42.5

solution.description: Take 75% of the 80-mile trip to get the distance covered at the faster rate.
Subtract the first-part distance from the total to get the remaining distance.
Apply D = RT to the first leg, dividing 60 miles by 45 miles per hour for its time.
Apply D = RT to the second leg, dividing 20 miles by 30 miles per hour for its time.
Add the two leg times to get the total time for the trip.
Divide the total distance by the total time to get the average speed.

key_reminders: Average speed is total distance divided by total time, not the average of the two rates.
Use D = RT separately on each leg because the rates differ.
The two leg times must be in the same unit before adding.
common_mistakes: Averaging 45 and 30 to get 37.5, which is choice (A).
Weighting the rates by distance share (0.75 \times 45 + 0.25 \times 30 = 41.25), which is choice (D), instead of by time.

concept.technique_name: base multiplication with deficiencies from base 1000

examples.problem_statement: Using base 1000 (the right-hand portion of the answer should therefore be of three digits), compute 978 \times 983 = ?

solution.result: deficiency of -22 for the first number
solution.description: Write the first number against base 1000 and record how far short of the base it falls.

solution.result: deficiency of -17 for the second number
solution.description: Do the same for the second number, recording its shortfall from 1000 beside it.
Cross-subtract: take one number minus the other number's deficiency to get the left-hand portion of the answer.
Multiply the two deficiencies to get the right-hand portion, padded to the three digits that base 1000 demands.
Join the left-hand and right-hand portions to read off the product.

key_reminders: With base 1000 the right-hand portion must carry exactly three digits.
The left-hand portion is one number minus the other number's deficiency (both cross-subtractions give the same value).
Both numbers are below the base, so the product of the two deficiencies is positive.
common_mistakes: Writing the right-hand part as 374 without checking it fills three digits, which breaks the moment the deficiency product is smaller (e.g. two digits).
Cross-subtracting with the wrong pairing, e.g. 978 - 22 or 983 - 17, instead of subtracting the other number's deficiency.
